pumac-2012-team-01.title: Diagonals and sides
pumac-2012-team-01.body:
The $5$ sides can never cross anything in the interior, so each is independently drawn or not: $2^5=32$ choices. The $5$ diagonals form a pentagram; two diagonals cross exactly when they share no endpoint, so each diagonal crosses exactly two others and the crossing relation is a $5$-cycle. We count sets of diagonals with no crossing pair, i.e. independent sets of a $5$-cycle: $1$ (empty) $+5$ (one diagonal) $+5$ (two non-crossing diagonals, i.e. two diagonals sharing an endpoint) $=11$.

So $N=32\cdot11=352$ and $N-64=288$.

**Answer: 288**

pumac-2012-team-02.title: Free digits
pumac-2012-team-02.body:
$10^{2012}$ has digit sum $1$, so only $2012$-digit strings (with leading zeros allowed, from $0$ to $10^{2012}-1$) matter. Choose the first $2011$ digits freely ($10^{2011}$ ways); exactly $2$ values of the last digit make the digit sum divisible by $5$. That gives $2\cdot10^{2011}$ strings, including the all-zero string which corresponds to $0$, not allowed. So $n=2\cdot10^{2011}-1=1999\ldots9$, with first three digits $199$.

**Answer: 199**

pumac-2012-team-03.title: Count digits

pumac-2012-team-04.title: Possible gcds
pumac-2012-team-04.body:
$2012=2^2\cdot503$, so a prime gcd is $2$ or $503$.

- $\gcd=2$: $n=2a$ with $a$ odd, $a\le1006$ (so $a\in\{1,3,\dots,1005\}$, $503$ values) and $503\nmid a$ (else the gcd would be $2\cdot503$): remove $a=503$, leaving $502$ values.
- $\gcd=503$: $n=503$ or $3\cdot503=1509$ ($n=2\cdot503$ and $4\cdot503$ have gcd $1006$ and $2012$): $2$ values.

Total $502+2=504$.

**Answer: 504**

pumac-2012-team-05.title: Distribution of the recorded number
pumac-2012-team-05.body:
With $n=10$: $256=25\cdot10+6$, so recorded values $1,\dots,6$ occur $26$ times each and $7,\dots,10$ occur $25$ times each. Hence
$$p=\frac{6\cdot26^2+4\cdot25^2}{256^2}=\frac{4056+2500}{2^{16}}=\frac{6556}{2^{16}},$$
and $p\cdot2^{16}=6556$.

**Answer: 6556**

pumac-2012-team-06.title: Winning and losing positions
pumac-2012-team-06.body:
Whoever can tell the opponent to go to the origin wins. We claim the player to move loses exactly when both coordinates are even.

- From a position with at least one odd coordinate, the mover can reach an (even, even) position: if $x,y$ are both odd go diagonally; if only $x$ is odd go left; if only $y$ is odd go down (and when the target is the origin, that wins immediately).
- From (even, even) every move leads to a position with an odd coordinate (a move changes one or both coordinates by $1$), so the opponent can again move to (even, even); the mover can never be the one who sends the opponent to the origin, since the origin is (even, even) and is only reachable from a position with an odd coordinate.

So you win iff at least one coordinate is odd. Among all $347^2$ points in the square, $174^2$ have both coordinates even (even values $0,2,\dots,346$: $174$ of them), so the winning starts number $347^2-174^2=120409-30276=90133$ (the origin is not a winning start and is among the even-even points, so it does not affect the count).

**Answer: 90133**

pumac-2012-team-07.title: Coordinates
pumac-2012-team-07.body:
The figure is symmetric about the perpendicular bisector of $BC$. Put $B=\left(-\frac{\sqrt2}2,0\right)$, $C=\left(\frac{\sqrt2}2,0\right)$. Then $A=B+\sqrt2(\cos120^\circ,\sin120^\circ)=\left(-\sqrt2,\frac{\sqrt6}2\right)$ and $D=\left(\sqrt2,\frac{\sqrt6}2\right)$. The side $AE$ makes $105^\circ$ with $AB$ (which points in direction $-60^\circ$), so $AE$ points in direction $45^\circ$ and meets the axis $x=0$ at $E=A+2(\cos45^\circ,\sin45^\circ)=\left(0,\frac{\sqrt6}2+\sqrt2\right)$.

Then $\vec{BD}=\left(\frac{3\sqrt2}2,\frac{\sqrt6}2\right)$ and $\vec{BE}=\left(\frac{\sqrt2}2,\frac{\sqrt6}2+\sqrt2\right)$, and
$$2[BDE]=\frac{3\sqrt2}{2}\left(\frac{\sqrt6}2+\sqrt2\right)-\frac{\sqrt6}2\cdot\frac{\sqrt2}2=\frac{3\sqrt3}{2}+3-\frac{\sqrt3}2=3+\sqrt3.$$
So $[BDE]=\frac{3+\sqrt3}{2}$, $a=3$, $b=3$, $c=2$ and $abc=18$.

**Answer: 18**

pumac-2012-team-08.title: Factor
pumac-2012-team-08.body:
Multiply by $x^2y^2$ and move everything to one side:
$$4x^4+20x^2y^2+25y^4-4022x^2-10055y^2-2012=0.$$
With $u=2x^2+5y^2$ this is $u^2-2011u-2012=(u-2012)(u+1)=0$. Since $u+1>0$, we need $2x^2+5y^2=2012$. Here $x,y\neq0$ and $5y^2\le2012$ gives $|y|\le20$; $2012-5y^2$ must be twice a perfect square, and the only possibility is $y^2=324$, $x^2=196$ (the other values of $y$ give $2012-5y^2$ that is odd or not twice a square). So $(x,y)=(\pm14,\pm18)$ and the maximum of $xy-1$ is $14\cdot18-1=251$.

**Answer: 251**

pumac-2012-team-09.title: Both axes must meet the square
pumac-2012-team-09.body:
The graph of $xy=0$ is the union of the two coordinate axes. The boundary of a convex region meets a line in at most $2$ points (unless it runs along a side), so to get at least $3$ points the boundary must meet both axes. A square of side $7\sqrt2$ centered at $(c_x,c_y)$ and rotated by $\theta$ has half-width $w(\theta)=\frac{7\sqrt2}2(|\cos\theta|+|\sin\theta|)$ in both coordinate directions; it meets both axes iff $|c_x|\le w(\theta)$ and $|c_y|\le w(\theta)$. The largest value of $w$ is $7$ (at $\theta=45^\circ$, where the square is a diamond with vertices at distance $7$ from its center along the axis directions). So the set of admissible centers is the square $|x|\le7$, $|y|\le7$, of area $14^2=196$.

**Answer: 196**

pumac-2012-team-10.title: Legendre's formula
pumac-2012-team-10.body:
The number of trailing zeros of $2012!$ is the exponent of $5$ in $2012!$ (there are more factors of $2$):
$$\left\lfloor\frac{2012}5\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac{2012}{25}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac{2012}{125}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac{2012}{625}\right\rfloor=402+80+16+3=501.$$

**Answer: 501**

pumac-2012-team-11.title: Relate the sums to A
pumac-2012-team-11.body:
$C=A-1$ and $E=D-1$, so $\frac CA=1-\frac1A$ and $\frac EA=\frac DA-\frac1A$ are irrational ($A$ is a rational multiple of $\pi^6$, hence $\frac1A$ is irrational), and $\frac BA$ is not rational either (given).

For $D$, split $A$ into odd and even terms: $A=D+\sum\frac1{(2n)^6}=D+\frac1{2^6}A$. So $\frac DA=1-\frac1{64}=\frac{63}{64}$, the rational one. Concatenating $r=63$ and $s=64$ gives $6364$.

**Answer: 6364**

pumac-2012-team-12.title: The cut curve of an elbow
pumac-2012-team-12.body:
Rolling the width-$2$ sheet gives a cylinder of circumference $2$, radius $\frac1\pi$. Two identical cylinders form a right-angle elbow when each is cut by a plane at $45^\circ$ to its axis. Measuring the angle $\varphi$ around the cylinder from the point where the cut is highest, the cut plane has height $r(1+\cos\varphi)$ above its lowest point, and on the unrolled sheet $\varphi=\pi x$. So $f(x)=\frac{1+\cos\pi x}{\pi}$, which indeed satisfies $f(\pm1)=0$.

Then $f\left(\frac13\right)=\frac{1+\frac12}\pi=\frac3{2\pi}$ and $f\left(\frac16\right)=\frac{1+\frac{\sqrt3}2}\pi=\frac{2+\sqrt3}{2\pi}$. The sum is $\frac{5+\sqrt3}{2\pi}$, so $a=5$, $b=3$, $c=2$ and $a+b+c=10$.

(The official key lists $532$, which is the concatenation $5,3,2$ of $a,b,c$; the crossword needed a three-digit entry.)

**Answer: 10**

pumac-2012-team-13.title: Perfect square and odd function
pumac-2012-team-13.body:
Since $x^2-4x+4=(x-2)^2$,
$$\Xi(x)=\left(139+(x-2)\sqrt{2012+e^{(x-2)^2}}\right)^2,$$
as expanding the square gives exactly the four terms. For $x\in[0,4]$ the quantity $(x-2)\sqrt{2012+e^{(x-2)^2}}$ has absolute value at most $2\sqrt{2012+e^4}<91$, so the bracket is positive and $\sqrt{\Xi(x)}=139+g(x-2)$ with $g(t)=t\sqrt{2012+e^{t^2}}$ an odd function. The area is
$$\int_0^4\left(139+g(x-2)\right)dx=139\cdot4+\int_{-2}^2g(t)\,dt=556+0=556.$$

**Answer: 556**

pumac-2012-team-14.title: Coordinates
pumac-2012-team-14.body:
Put the base centers at $c_1=(0,0)$, $c_2=(4,0)$ and $c_3=(2,\sqrt{21})$ (distances $2+2=4$, $2+3=5$, $2+3=5$). The cone apexes are $P_1=(0,0,4)$, $P_2=(4,0,4)$, $P_3=(2,\sqrt{21},6)$, and the fourth vertex is $Q=(2,\sqrt{21},0)$, the center of the base of the third cone.

From $Q$ the vector to $P_3$ is vertical, $(0,0,6)$. So $V=\frac16\left|\left(\overrightarrow{QP_1}\times\overrightarrow{QP_2}\right)\cdot\overrightarrow{QP_3}\right|=\frac16\cdot6\cdot\left|(c_1-c_3)\times(c_2-c_3)\right|$, which is twice the area of triangle $c_1c_2c_3$. This triangle has sides $5,5,4$, altitude $\sqrt{21}$ and area $2\sqrt{21}$. So $V=4\sqrt{21}$ and $V^2=16\cdot21=336$.

**Answer: 336**

pumac-2012-team-15.title: Painting time vs total time
pumac-2012-team-15.body:
Together they paint at $1+\frac16=\frac76$ houses per hour, so painting one house takes $\frac67$ hours of actual work. The remaining $7-\frac67=\frac{43}7$ hours are spent texting. The probability is $\frac{43/7}{7}=\frac{43}{49}$, and $r+s=43+49=92$.

**Answer: 92**

pumac-2012-team-16.title: Find the pattern
pumac-2012-team-16.body:
Compute $(a_2,b_2)=(2,2+2\sqrt2)$, $(a_3,b_3)=(2\sqrt2,4+2\sqrt2)$. We claim $(a_n,b_n)=(\sqrt2)^n\,(1,1+\sqrt2)$ for $n\ge2$: it holds for $n=2$, and if true for $n$ then $a_{n+1}=|a_n-b_n|=(\sqrt2)^n\sqrt2=(\sqrt2)^{n+1}$ and $b_{n+1}=(\sqrt2)^n(2+\sqrt2)=(\sqrt2)^{n+1}(1+\sqrt2)$.

With $r=\frac{a_n}{b_n}$, the expression is $\frac{r^2+r-6}{6-r^2}=-1+\frac r{6-r^2}$, which is increasing in $r$ on $(0,\sqrt6)$. We have $r_1=1+\sqrt2$ and $r_n=\frac1{1+\sqrt2}=\sqrt2-1$ for $n\ge2$, so the minimum is at $r=\sqrt2-1$:
$$-1+\frac{\sqrt2-1}{3+2\sqrt2}=-1+(\sqrt2-1)(3-2\sqrt2)=-1+5\sqrt2-7=5\sqrt2-8.$$
So $a=5$, $b=2$, $c=8$ and concatenating $c,b,a$ gives $825$.

**Answer: 825**

pumac-2012-team-17.title: Fermat's Last Theorem
pumac-2012-team-17.body:
Write the equation as $a^{503}+(b^2)^{503}=(c^4)^{503}$. By Fermat's Last Theorem this has no solution in nonzero integers, so one of $a$, $b^2$, $c^4$ is $0$, i.e. one of $a,b,c$ is $0$.

- $a=0$: $b^{1006}=c^{2012}$ gives $|b|=c^2$. Since $c^2<2012$, $|c|\le44$. For $c=0$ we get $b=0$; for each of the $88$ nonzero $c$ there are two values $b=\pm c^2$: $1+176=177$ solutions.
- $b=0$: $a^{503}=c^{2012}$ gives $a=c^4<2012$, so $|c|\le6$: $13$ solutions.
- $c=0$: $a^{503}=-b^{1006}$ gives $a=-b^2$, $|b|\le44$: $89$ solutions.

The triple $(0,0,0)$ lies in all three sets and no other triple lies in two of them, so the total is $177+13+89-2=277$.

**Answer: 277**
